The practical point is hiring. The plan needs {{Italy.hires_scenario}} hires instead of {{Italy.hires_base}}, which is {{Italy.hires_change}} more, and they have to be in place before the surge lands. Each agent handles {{rules.capacity_per_agent}} advertisers at a time over a {{rules.support_days}}-day support window, so late hiring would push waits toward the {{rules.max_wait_days}}-day limit. The Germany plan is fairly robust to lower sign-ups but quite sensitive to higher ones. If volume runs above forecast, the current staffing of {{demand_100.current_plan.avg_active}} active agents stops keeping up. Mean wait is {{demand_100.current_plan.mean_wait_days}} days at forecast, rises to {{demand_110.current_plan.mean_wait_days}} days with a modest overshoot, and reaches {{demand_120.current_plan.mean_wait_days}} days with a bigger one. At the top of the range it hits {{demand_130.current_plan.mean_wait_days}} days, and the service rate slips to {{demand_130.current_plan.service_rate}}.

Replanning removes most of that risk at a small cost. At the top of the range the replanned staffing averages {{demand_130.replanned.avg_active}} active agents, holds wait at {{demand_130.replanned.mean_wait_days}} days, and keeps service at {{demand_130.replanned.service_rate}}. Total cost goes from {{demand_130.current_plan.total_cost}} to {{demand_130.replanned.total_cost}}, and net value is {{demand_130.replanned.net_value}} against {{demand_130.current_plan.net_value}} for the unchanged plan. On the downside, the current plan still costs {{demand_70.current_plan.total_cost}} at the low end. Replanning trims that to {{demand_70.replanned.total_cost}} with {{demand_70.replanned.avg_active}} agents, lifting net value from {{demand_70.current_plan.net_value}} to {{demand_70.replanned.net_value}}.

In practice, watch actual sign-ups against forecast and set a trigger to add capacity once they run about a tenth ahead. That is where waits start to climb ({{demand_110.current_plan.mean_wait_days}} days) but before they become painful. The unchanged plan can look slightly better on net value in the high scenarios, for example {{demand_120.current_plan.net_value}} against {{demand_120.replanned.net_value}} at a fifth above forecast. That gain comes from advertisers waiting longer, so I would not treat it as a saving.

Yes, the Poland plan holds up in both directions: at 20% lower sign ups it just runs with spare capacity, and at 20% higher it still serves everyone, though waits stretch. At the lower volume, the current plan keeps service at {{demand_80.current_plan.service_rate}} with a mean wait of {{demand_80.current_plan.mean_wait_days}} days and net value of {{demand_80.current_plan.net_value}}. Replanning would trim average active agents to {{demand_80.replanned.avg_active}}, down from {{demand_80.current_plan.avg_active}}. The higher side is where the plan gets stressed. With the current staffing, mean wait rises to {{demand_120.current_plan.mean_wait_days}} days, still well inside the {{rules.max_wait_days}}-day limit, and service stays at {{demand_120.current_plan.service_rate}}. Replanning would bring the wait back to {{demand_120.replanned.mean_wait_days}} days by raising average active agents to {{demand_120.replanned.avg_active}}. The cost is {{demand_120.replanned.total_cost}} against {{demand_120.current_plan.total_cost}}, and net value comes out at {{demand_120.replanned.net_value}} versus {{demand_120.current_plan.net_value}}. So adding agents buys much faster service, but it doesn't raise net value in this case.

Practically, I'd keep the current plan and set a trigger to add agents if sign ups trend above forecast. Beyond the 20% case the plan starts to break: at the top of the tested range the current plan's mean wait reaches {{demand_130.current_plan.mean_wait_days}} days and service falls to {{demand_130.current_plan.service_rate}}. Replanning there restores {{demand_130.replanned.service_rate}} service with a {{demand_130.replanned.mean_wait_days}}-day wait.

Net value in Turkey rises with demand under both plans, but replanning is what keeps it clean at the top end. In the lowest-demand case, net value is {{demand_70.replanned.net_value}} replanned versus {{demand_70.current_plan.net_value}} on the current plan. In the highest-demand case it reaches {{demand_130.replanned.net_value}} replanned versus {{demand_130.current_plan.net_value}} on the current plan.

The current plan holds headcount fixed at {{demand_100.current_plan.avg_active}} active agents, so extra demand turns into waiting. Mean wait is {{demand_110.current_plan.mean_wait_days}} days in the first step above forecast and {{demand_120.current_plan.mean_wait_days}} in the next. In the highest case it is {{demand_130.current_plan.mean_wait_days}} days, and the service rate slips to {{demand_130.current_plan.service_rate}}. That holds wait at {{demand_130.replanned.mean_wait_days}} days and service at {{demand_130.replanned.service_rate}}, for a total cost of {{demand_130.replanned.total_cost}} against {{demand_130.current_plan.total_cost}}. The practical point is that the fixed plan looks fine up to roughly forecast, but it has little buffer above it. Waits are already {{demand_120.current_plan.mean_wait_days}} days in the second step above forecast, and the {{rules.max_wait_days}}-day maximum wait is close at the top end. UAE has the most volatile monthly demand, with a monthly coefficient of variation of {{insight.top_monthly_cv}}, the highest of any country. I can't rank the other countries from what I have here, so UAE is the only one I'd single out.

Day-to-day noise doesn't separate countries, because it's high everywhere, with a median daily coefficient of variation of {{insight.median_daily_cv}}. Daily swings are largely a fact of life for every team, while UAE's month-to-month swings are the real outlier.

In practice, I'd size every team on monthly demand rather than reacting to daily spikes. For UAE I'd keep some flexible capacity in reserve, since cutting headcount after a peak is costly (the cost share is {{rules.fire_cost_share}}), and a flexible buffer is cheaper than hiring and then letting people go.

Sign-ups peak in November, when demand runs at {{insight.peak_index}} of the average month in {{plan.year}}.

The low point is June, at {{insight.low_index}} of average. That makes the swing between the quietest and busiest months large, so a headcount sized for the average month would be too thin in November and too generous in June.

In practice, I'd have any extra capacity trained and ready before November starts, rather than hiring into the peak. I'd also avoid sizing permanent headcount to November, since that capacity would sit underused around June. Temporary or flexible cover for the peak is the safer way to stay within the {{rules.max_wait_days}}-day maximum wait.

An advertiser can wait in the pool for up to {{rules.max_wait_days}} days. If no agent slot opens by then, they are removed from the pool and never receive support [rules.md / Waiting pool].

The clock only matters when no slot is free. If an agent has capacity (each agent handles {{rules.capacity_per_agent}} advertisers at a time), the advertiser is assigned at once and doesn't wait at all.

In practice, I'd track two numbers: the service rate, meaning the share of eligible sign-ups in {{plan.year}} who get an agent before the wait runs out [kpis.md / Service rate], and wait time, reported as the mean and the 90th percentile for those who were assigned [kpis.md / Wait time]. If the 90th percentile creeps toward the limit, you are close to losing advertisers to removal and should look at capacity.

Firing an agent costs {{rules.fire_cost_share}} of that agent's annual salary for each notice given [kpis.md / Firing cost].

The charge lands in the month the notice is given, and every notice in the plan falls in January, so the timing doesn't change the {{plan.year}} firing cost [assumptions.md / A5 Notice month]. The agent is still paid for the notice month and keeps serving the advertisers already assigned, but takes no new ones, so nobody loses support halfway through. That notice-month salary comes on top of the firing cost.

Both the salary and the firing cost are deducted from expected uplift value when we calculate net value for the year [kpis.md / Net value]. I can't give you a currency figure here because the notes don't include salary levels, but if you give me the salary for the agents you're considering, the cost is simply that salary times {{rules.fire_cost_share}}.

Service rate is the share of eligible advertisers who sign up in {{plan.year}} and are assigned an agent before their {{rules.max_wait_days}} day wait runs out. Timing within that window doesn't matter, so someone assigned on the last allowed day still counts as served [kpis.md / Service rate].

It measures whether advertisers get served at all, not how quickly. Waiting doesn't reduce uplift unless the {{rules.max_wait_days}} day limit is passed. The optimizer still prefers earlier service through a small weekly penalty on uplift, because the brief asks for timely support. That choice gives up a little simulated value but cuts the average wait noticeably [assumptions.md / A9 Waiting and value].

If you need a guaranteed minimum, the service level variant of the optimizer adds a floor on the share of eligible advertisers served. Each served advertiser occupies an agent slot for the {{rules.support_days}} day support period, so raising the floor means more headcount.

We assume the waiting pool is empty on 1 January [assumptions.md / A3 Pool on 1 January]. The brief only says agents start with no advertisers, and the history doesn't record who was still waiting on 31 December, so there was nothing reliable to carry over.

Starting empty is also the conservative choice. If the advertisers who signed up in the last {{rules.max_wait_days}} days of history were still waiting, the pool would open with a very large number of people. Net value would rise noticeably, and the January plan would change a lot. Remember too that anyone still unassigned after {{rules.max_wait_days}} days is dropped and never gets support [rules.md / Waiting pool], so a real backlog would matter quickly.

If you know the actual backlog at year end, give me the rough size and I can rerun January with it. Otherwise, treat January staffing as a cautious baseline, and expect that a real carryover would push early demand higher.
